opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it came down to what each one actually measures. GPA tells you how well you did on a set of exams that somebody else designed, under rules somebody else set. It's a fine signal for whether you can absorb material and perform under those conditions, but past a certain point, the difference between a 3.8 and a 3.9 says very little about whether you can build something new or solve a problem nobody has solved before.

Papers, competitions, and GitHub projects are different because they're open-ended. With a paper, you have to find a question worth asking and convince other people your answer matters. In a competition, you're up against real opponents and the scoreboard doesn't care about your excuses. And with open-source work, GitHub stars are almost brutally honest. Nobody stars your repo because you worked hard. They star it because it's useful to them. That feedback comes from the outside world, not from a grading rubric.

For me, that was a lot more motivating. When I was working on things like my reinforcement learning library, I could see people actually using it, filing issues, sending pull requests. That loop of building something, getting real feedback, and improving it taught me far more than optimizing for a few extra points on a final exam would have.

I also think it was a bit of a mindset shift. Once you stop treating GPA as the main scoreboard, you start asking: what will still matter in five years? Nobody in industry or research asks for your transcript after your first job. But the code you wrote, the problems you solved, the things people still use, those compound. So I tried to spend my time on things that compound.

That said, I don't want to tell students to ignore grades completely. They still open certain doors. It's more about not letting them become the only thing you optimize for.

r001.rationale: The response favors work the speaker chooses to pursue and use as their own measure of progress over treating GPA as the main scoreboard.

r002.rationale: It describes open-source work as useful and a source of real feedback, but does not say contributing to the community distinguishes someone from others.

r003.rationale: It says code, problems solved, and projects that people use compound over time, and describes that work as more valuable than optimizing for extra GPA points.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to what each number actually measures. GPA tells you how well you can do what someone else already defined. The exam has an answer key, the course has a syllabus, and the ceiling is fixed. You can be perfect at it and still have produced nothing that exists in the world.

Papers, competitions, and GitHub stars all share one property: they're judged by people who have no obligation to care about you. A reviewer doesn't know you. A leaderboard doesn't give partial credit for effort. Someone starring a repo at 2 a.m. in a different country is doing it because the code solved their problem. That feedback is noisy and sometimes unfair, but it's honest in a way grades aren't.

For me it started with Tianshou, honestly. I built it as a student because I wanted a reinforcement learning library I actually enjoyed using. Nobody assigned it. When people started opening issues and submitting pull requests, I realized I was getting evaluated on something real: did I design a good abstraction, did I write documentation someone could follow, did I respond to a bug report well. No course grades you on that, and yet it's most of what the job actually is.

The other thing is that those external signals compound. A good grade is consumed the moment it's recorded. A paper leads to a collaborator, a competition result leads to a conversation, a repo leads to a user who becomes a contributor. So it's not just a different scoreboard, it's a scoreboard that opens doors while you're playing.

I'd add one caveat, though. I don't think stars are intrinsically meaningful either. They can be gamed, and they reward things that are popular rather than things that are deep. The point was never to replace one vanity metric with another. It was to pick metrics that forced me to build and ship, because that's the habit I wanted, and GPA never demanded it.

r001.rationale: The response says the point was to “pick metrics” that required building and shipping, contrasting that choice with GPA as a system that never demanded it.

r002.rationale: It describes building Tianshou and receiving issues and pull requests, but does not identify open-source contribution as a way to distinguish oneself from others.

r003.rationale: It contrasts grades that are “consumed” once recorded with papers and repositories that compound into collaborators, users, contributors, and opportunities, and favors building and shipping.

astra-6.text:
For me, papers, competitions, and GitHub stars felt more connected to what I could actually create. GPA tells you how well you perform within a course, but I wanted to know: Can I explore a problem without a predefined answer? Can I build something that works? Does someone else find it useful?

Those other measures aren’t perfect either. A star count doesn’t capture the full value of a project, just as a grade doesn’t capture the full value of a person. But they gave me more meaningful feedback on the kind of work I wanted to do, and more ownership over how I learned.

r001.rationale: The response says the alternative measures gave the speaker more ownership over how they learned, supporting a self-directed evaluation system over relying on GPA alone.

r002.rationale: It mentions GitHub stars and useful projects, but does not identify contributing to open source as a way to distinguish oneself.

r003.rationale: It contrasts GPA with creating and building, but does not claim that developing a distinctive body of work is more valuable for long-term development than spending substantial time maximizing GPA.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it was about having something concrete to show for what I’d learned. GPA can tell you how well you did in a course, but I wanted to know whether I could take an idea and actually do something with it. Papers, competitions, and projects on GitHub gave me different ways to test that and get feedback beyond the classroom.

Of course, those metrics have limitations too. A star count doesn’t tell you everything about a project. What felt more meaningful was the work behind them: could I solve a problem, build something useful, and explain it well enough for other people to engage with it?

r001.rationale: The candidate compares GPA with concrete work and feedback, but does not advocate choosing a self-defined evaluation system over one imposed by others.

r002.rationale: It mentions GitHub projects and stars, but does not identify contributing to the open-source community as a way to distinguish oneself.

r003.rationale: The candidate values work behind metrics, but does not say building a distinctive body of work is more valuable for long-term development than spending substantial time maximizing GPA.
